source.title: Deep Transformers without Shortcuts: Modifying Self-attention for Faithful Signal Propagation
source.authors: B. He; James Martens; Guodong Zhang; Aleksandar Botev; Andy Brock; Samuel L. Smith; Y. Teh

record.tranche_reason: Tests deep-transformer trainability in a new architecture and language-modeling setting, including shortcutless and normalization-free models.
record.gate_note: The study reports training-loss and validation-perplexity results for its own transformer methods and baselines. Cited results from other studies are not recorded as rows. It does not measure classification error on CIFAR or test random labels.
record.test_reason: The initialization ablations test V4's signal-preservation and training-speed relationship in plain transformers, a new architecture and language-modeling setting. Transformer shortcut experiments do not test V3's convolutional-network claim, and RMSNorm comparisons do not test V6's batch-normalization or Fixup claims.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors conclude that attention modifications enabling faithful signal propagation make deep vanilla transformers trainable. E-SPA reaches standard-transformer performance after roughly five times more iterations, and with normalized skips can match standard training speed without normalization. Qualify Value-SkipInit as retaining a value-path shortcut, and distinguish the paper's inconsistent training-versus-validation descriptions of the longer-training figures.
record.recipe_differences: Modifies self-attention initialization and computation using bias matrices and location-dependent rescaling; uses language-modeling loss on WikiText-103 and C4 rather than image classification.
record.method_sensitivity: Attention modification (E-SPA, U-SPA, Value-SkipInit), normalization, activation, depth, query/key initialization scale, and training duration affect results.

fits_no_version.finding: Unmodified deep skipless transformers fail to train, while modified attention enables training; vanilla E-SPA reaches standard-transformer performance after roughly five times more iterations.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Signal-preserving attention modifications enable deep shortcutless decoder transformers to train, with a substantial iteration cost relative to standard residual transformers.

fits_no_version.finding: E-SPA transformers with normalized skips can match standard-transformer performance without RMSNorm.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Modified attention and appropriately weighted shortcuts can remove RMSNorm while preserving transformer training speed in the tested settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Removing RMSNorm has mixed effects across attention methods and activations in skipless transformers.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The training benefit of RMSNorm in modified skipless transformers depends on attention design and activation.

fits_no_version.finding: Deeper vanilla E-SPA transformers train more slowly initially, but longer training largely closes or reverses the depth gap.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Depth-dependent optimization delays in vanilla E-SPA transformers can diminish with longer training.

record.problems: The reported experiments concern language modeling rather than classification; several comparisons are only plotted; most reported results evaluate the authors' modified attention methods rather than unmodified shortcutless transformers.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted due to the 60-row limit. Figure-only comparisons without a textual result description were not transcribed as numeric outcomes.

untested.parts: CIFAR convolutional-network training classification error, random or corrupted labels, and model-size or regularization effects.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student optimization, spurious minima, and extra student neurons.
Plain versus residual batch-normalized convolutional networks on ImageNet or CIFAR-10, including persistence with longer training; the named tanh and Fixup exceptions.

The named activation-matched feedforward-network settings, orthogonal versus Gaussian very deep tanh networks, 10,000-layer convolutional networks, and a controlled initialization comparison establishing increased maximum trainable depth.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, curvature dynamics, catapult recovery, edge of stability, and divergence.
Batch-normalization effects on accuracy gain and learning-rate tolerance, and residual-network training with Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: V3 and V6 links were removed because their specified architectures or normalization methods were not tested. States for rows linked to none indicate inability to determine a listed version's effect, not uncertainty about the reported transformer result. No external sources or files were consulted.

versions.untested_parts: CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100 classification error, corrupted or random labels, and model size effects.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student problems and student width relative to teacher width.
ImageNet/CIFAR-10 convolutional networks, batch normalization specifically, and the named tanh and Fixup methods.
Activation-matched initializations in plain feedforward networks, deep tanh networks, and 10,000-layer convolutional networks.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, curvature or sharpness, and loss spikes or divergence above the threshold.
Batch normalization, sigmoid networks on MNIST, VGG on CIFAR-10, Inception on ImageNet, and Fixup.

rows.subject: E-SPA vanilla transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared orthogonal parameter initialization with Gaussian fan-in initialization.
rows.value: Orthogonal initialization slightly outperforms Gaussian fan-in initialization (by around 0.15 train loss).
rows.uncertainty: not stated
rows.locator: Appendix G, Ablation over orthogonal initialisation; Figure 9
rows.note: The stated difference is small; figure does not provide exact per-condition values in text.
rows.check: The approximately 0.15 training-loss advantage is explicitly small. This extends the general initialization claim to transformers; it does not test the specific tanh result.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix G, orthogonal-initialization ablation; Figure 9; Appendix H.1.

rows.subject: E-SPA vanilla transformer
rows.operation_detail: Varied the orthogonal initialization scale of query and key weights.
rows.value: For small initialisation scales, there is little effect of varying initial scale.
rows.uncertainty: Mean and error bars over 3 seeds; no exact values stated in text
rows.locator: Appendix G, Sensitivity to query-key initialisation scale; Figure 8
rows.note: The text describes a negligible effect at small scales.
rows.check: Small query/key scales produce little performance difference. This is absence of sensitivity within that range, not absence of successful training or signal preservation.

source_check.correct: Little training-loss sensitivity among small query/key initialization scales; these scales all approximately preserve the intended attention initialization. State relative to V4: cannot_determine.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.3; Appendix G, query-key initialization-scale sensitivity; Figure 8.
source_check.problem: Negligible sensitivity among signal-preserving initializations does not establish absence of V4's benefit from signal-preserving initialization.

rows.subject: E-SPA vanilla transformer
rows.operation_detail: Varied the orthogonal initialization scale of query and key weights.
rows.value: Training performance degrades at larger scales.
rows.uncertainty: Mean and error bars over 3 seeds; no exact values stated in text
rows.locator: Appendix G, Sensitivity to query-key initialisation scale; Figure 8
rows.note: Authors attribute this to less precise attention-matrix reverse engineering at larger scales.
rows.check: Larger scales degrade the intended initial attention matrices and worsen training, consistent with V4's direction. The recorded reversed state incorrectly treats increasing scale as the predicted beneficial intervention.

source_check.locator_found: Appendix G, query-key initialization-scale sensitivity; Figure 8.
